opus-5.5.text:
I often frame it with an analogy. Robotics today feels a lot like autonomous driving around 2015 or 2016, and also a bit like language models just before GPT-3.

On the autonomous driving side, around then people had seen convincing demos. Cars could drive themselves on a highway or around a few city blocks, and suddenly everyone believed full autonomy was two or three years away. Money poured in, a lot of companies were founded, and then the field ran into the long tail: the endless rare situations that a demo never shows you. It took close to another decade of data collection, engineering, safety validation and operational work before you got real driverless services running at scale in a handful of cities. Robotics is at that demo moment now. You see videos of robots folding laundry, making coffee, doing backflips, and they're genuinely impressive, but there's a big gap between a demo that works some of the time and a product that works reliably enough that someone will pay for it and trust it in their home or factory.

On the foundation model side, the analogy is about the recipe. In language, people eventually found a recipe that scaled: a simple architecture, a simple objective, and a huge amount of data from the internet. Once that recipe was clear, progress became somewhat predictable. You add compute and data and things get better. In robotics we have strong hints that a similar recipe exists. Vision-language-action models, large-scale imitation learning, and pretraining on diverse robot data all show real generalization. But we haven't hit the point where the scaling curve is clean and everyone agrees on it. And the biggest difference is data. Language had the internet sitting there for free. Robotics has no internet of physical interaction. Every hour of robot data has to be collected, through teleoperation, simulation, human videos, or deployed robots, and each of those sources has its own problems.

So my honest read is that we're early but no longer at zero. Compared with autonomous driving, robotics is harder in some ways: far more diverse tasks, contact-rich manipulation, and hardware that isn't standardized the way a car is. It's easier in others. Many applications are lower stakes than a car at 100 kilometers an hour, so a robot can make a mistake, retry, or ask for help. Compared with LLMs, we have the advantage of borrowing a lot from them. Vision and language understanding come almost for free now, so the robot already knows what a cup is and what "put it in the sink" means. The hard part that's left is the physical part: dexterity, robustness, and closing the loop with the real world.

If I had to sum it up, the next few years will be about whoever figures out the data flywheel: getting robots deployed in narrow but real settings, collecting data from that use, and feeding it back into the models. That's what eventually made autonomous driving work, and that's what made language models take off once the data existed. Robotics has to build that flywheel almost from scratch, and I think that's the most exciting and also the most humbling part of where we are.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, robotics right now is roughly where autonomous driving was around 2016 or 2017, with one important difference in how the foundation model era changes the recipe.

If you remember driving at that time, everyone had demos. You could put a car on a highway, run it in a geofenced area, show a beautiful video. And the industry collectively underestimated the long tail. It took almost a decade from "the demo works" to Waymo actually operating as a business in a handful of cities. The gap was not the perception stack or the planner in isolation. It was data, closed-loop evaluation, safety cases, and the brutal engineering of making the system behave consistently across millions of edge cases.

Robotics is in that demo-rich moment now. Humanoids folding laundry, arms doing dexterous manipulation, pick-and-place in warehouses. The videos are real, but most of them are narrow, heavily teleoperated for data collection, and far from the reliability you need to deploy without a person nearby. So in terms of maturity, I would say we are at the "it works sometimes in the lab, we have found the shape of the problem" stage, not the "we know how to scale" stage.

Now, what foundation models change. In driving, the whole industry started modular and only later moved toward end-to-end learned systems. Robotics gets to skip some of that. People are starting with large pretrained vision-language models and asking them to output actions directly. That gives you something driving did not have early on, which is a prior over the world. The model already knows what a cup is, what "put it on the shelf" means, roughly how objects behave. That generalization is genuinely new, and it is why I am more optimistic about the timeline than a naive driving analogy would suggest.

But there is a structural problem. Language models had the internet. Driving had fleets of cars logging every mile. Robotics has neither. There is no internet of robot actions, and there are no million-unit fleets yet. So the bottleneck is not model architecture, it is the data flywheel. Whoever figures out how to get robots deployed in enough places doing useful enough work that the data collects itself, that is the company that wins. Everything before that, teleop farms, simulation, video pretraining, those are ways of bootstrapping until the flywheel turns.

So my short answer: the models have given us the ability to generalize earlier than driving ever could, but the deployment and data problem is still the same decade-long grind. I would be skeptical of anyone saying general-purpose humanoids in homes in two years, and equally skeptical of anyone saying this is just hype. The honest position is that we have the first real foundation, and now it is an industrial problem as much as a research one.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics is at a stage where foundation models have opened up new possibilities, but we’re still figuring out how to turn those possibilities into reliable systems in the physical world.

Autonomous driving is a useful comparison because it shows how large the gap can be between a compelling demonstration and something you can trust every day. A robot also has to perceive its environment, make decisions, and act under uncertainty. But with a general-purpose robot, the tasks and environments can vary much more. Driving has a relatively clear objective; “help me around the house” is much harder to define and evaluate.

Foundation models give us a promising starting point. They can help robots interpret instructions, recognize objects, and use knowledge across tasks. But understanding what should happen doesn’t automatically mean being able to make it happen. Grasping an unfamiliar object, dealing with contact, or recovering when something slips requires physical experience and feedback.

So I’d separate progress in the model from progress in the whole robotic system. We may see capabilities improve quickly, while dependable deployment takes longer. My expectation is that useful robots will first succeed in tasks with clear boundaries, and broader capabilities will grow from that experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics is at a stage where autonomous driving offers useful lessons, while foundation models are opening up new possibilities.

Autonomous driving shows how difficult it is to turn an impressive demonstration into a reliable system. You need data, simulation, hardware, and a continuous feedback loop from real-world operation. Robotics faces those same challenges, but often with less standardized hardware and much more varied tasks. A robot manipulating objects has to deal with contact, friction, and things moving in ways it cannot fully observe.

Foundation models help because they give robots a broader starting point for perception, language understanding, and potentially action. Instead of building every task separately, we can begin to share capabilities across tasks. But understanding an instruction is still different from executing it reliably in the physical world.

So I would distinguish progress in general capabilities from readiness for deployment. We’re seeing exciting progress in the first, while the second still requires a lot of engineering and real-world learning. The key question is whether we can build a loop where deployed robots collect useful experience, that experience improves the model, and the improved model makes the robots more useful.
